headline: Approved a temporary moratorium on data centers; tabled the FY27 budget true-up and Chief McNamara's contract amendment.

METHUEN CITY COUNCIL REGULAR MEETING MINUTES                                     
Tuesday, September 8, 2026 @ 7:00 P.M.   
GREAT HALL, SEARLES BUILDING 
 
1. Roll Call - members present – Clr. MacLaren, Clr. Marsan, Clr. Pesce, Clr. Simard, 
Clr. Valley, Clr. Drew and Chair Soto – 2 absent (Clr. DiZoglio & Clr. Santos) 
 
2. Acceptance of the Agenda - Motion to accept by Clr. Pesce, seconded by Clr. Simard 
– UPON VOTE – unanimously approved - 2 absent (Clr. DiZoglio & Clr. Santos) 
 
3. Pledge of Allegiance/Invocation/Moment of Silence – Chair Soto recognized Vice 
Chair Pesce, “I'm going to read some words of wisdom by John F. Kennedy. Leadership 
and learning are indispensable to each other.” Chair Soto then recognized Clr. Pesce to 
deliver a moment of silence, “Actually, if everybody could just remain standing. I 
apologize. I was just thinking --- I didn't receive any requests for a moment of silence, 
but Jason Dinella, who was a close family friend and played in the 1992 historic 
Methuen football game where they won, recently passed away. He left his beautiful wife, 
his two boys, and I would like to have a moment of silence for them.”  
 
4. Public Participation 
• Diane Moore, 58 Lowell Boulevard, Methuen, “Good evening, everyone. City 
Council, everyone present in the room, the Mayor's not here, unfortunately. I'd like to 
take a moment tonight to talk about something that I believe belongs to every citizen of 
Methuen, the Edward F. Searles Estate. This Saturday, September 12th, the estate will 
once again open its doors for tours as part of the Trails and Sails program. The tours are 
from 10 to 3 in the afternoon. This is a wonderful opportunity for the residents to step 
inside and experience one of Methuen's most extraordinary historical treasures. The 
estate is more than a beautiful property. It represents an important part of Methuen's 
history and remarkable architecture, craftsmanship, artwork, and stories behind the walls 
that every citizen deserves to hear and share. It's part of who we are. The Friends of the 
Searles estate, which I sit president as soon as the 501c is completed, the Friends of the 
Searles estate has been very hard in working to bring attention to the remarkable 
property, not just to preserve the past, but to imagine what it could mean for the future 
of the city. Because preservation isn't all about keeping something frozen in its time. It's 
about making sure that the next generation can experience what the last generation has 
left behind. This Saturday, tours provide the opportunity to see what the possibilities 
could be for you. I encourage the Mayor, who's not here tonight, and every one of you to 
bring your families. We do have the tours fully booked. However, if you show up, I'm at 
the check-in table and I will get you in. (Councilor) Ella (MacLaren) is coming to 
volunteer, I understand. Thank you. When you walk through the rooms, you look at the 
craftsmanship, you listen to the stories and the history that we have newly uncovered. 
And most importantly, you'll see what we really have in this city. Sometimes we don't 
realize what we have until we're in the room. This was my grammar school, imagine. 
There used to be a stage here and we used to have plays and things when I was in 
grammar school. We have something special in We have something worth saving and 
preserving. And I believe --- this is my opinion and a lot of people's opinion in the city, 
we have something worth to believe in, to give to our children and grandchildren. It's 
part of who we are. So, I have special invites for everyone, and I hope I see you on 
Saturday.” 
• Mary Beth Donovan Grassi, 15 Coolidge Street, Methuen – “Good evening, everyone 
and welcome back to school. Almost two years ago, Representative Ryan Hamilton,

who's here this evening, Krista McLeod, then director of the Nevins Memorial Library, 
and I began a conversation about something we all believe is fundamental to a child's 
success, literacy. That conversation became the Methuen Literacy Partnership, a 
community-driven initiative dedicated to ensuring that every child in Methuen has the 
foundational reading skills they need to succeed in school and in life. We believe that 
teaching reading, supporting literacy is not a responsibility that should lie solely on the 
schools, but should engage the entire community. We believe it takes a village to raise a 
reader. Since then, we have had meetings, gathered information through community 
surveys and conversations, engaged two consultants to help us better understand the data 
and shape our outreach, and launched three working groups focused on turning what we 
have learned into action. As part of that work, we are respectfully asking the city council 
to approve tonight the Mayor-designated funding for a Methuen Waterford Upstart pre-k 
pilot. Upstart is a home-based early learning and kindergarten readiness program that 
provides individualized interactive activities in reading, math, and science, along with 
caregiver support. It is a proven research-based program with a strong track record of 
helping young children in several states develop their early literacy skills they need to 
succeed in school. The funding will be administered through the Nevins Memorial 
Library, with the YMCA serving as a trusted community partner. They'll be doing 
outreach, enrollment, family engagement, and connections. Families will receive 
coaching in their home language, along with technical support. Devices and internet 
access may also be provided if the families have a need for them. We want to ensure that 
technology and access is not a barrier to education. The Early Childhood Working 
Group is discussing events throughout the school year to bring these families together in 
person beyond the screen to work together. We will measure the pilot's success in a 
variety of ways through enrollment and retention, caregiver feedback, and reading 
assessments before, during, and after the program. At its conclusion, the steering 
committee will share a report to help inform future decisions and possible next steps. 
Please know the approval of this pilot does not create an obligation for permanent city 
funding. We are grateful to the Castle Fund for its grant support, to Mayor Beauregard 
for recognizing the need and support for this effort, to the Nevins Memorial Library, 
who has been a partner since day one, and to Superintendent Galatsky, whose 
enthusiasm and support and willingness to work has made much of this possible. The 
Methuen Literacy Partnership is committed to keeping our community informed and 
involved. More information about our work can be found online and, on our website, 
and on our social media pages. Our community engagement group will be at Methuen 
Day, distributing books to all our younger residents, and I hope you will read about and 
join our Book Buddies pilot program, which is set to launch in a month. We'll be 
engaging with third-grade students at the Tenney School, and we hope to expand that 
engagement. We do believe it takes a village to raise a reader, and we look forward to 
your support. Thank you.” 
• Christina, 1 Riverview Boulevard, Pride’s Crossing Condominiums, Methuen – “My 
name is Christina. I live at 1 Riverview Boulevard at Price Crossing Condominiums. 
Apologies for not signing. I didn't realize we had to do that. I've never been here before, 
before all of you, so nice to meet you. What made me come here today was the data 
centers. I hear that the mayor is proposing a one-year moratorium, which I greatly 
support. I support, among some other people as well, a ban on the data centers. I know 
that Lowell right now is going through some hard times with the data center that was

put in. There were some lies that they were told, and a lot of enjoyment in their life has 
been taken from them. I would urge you to please look at the potential environmental 
and life impacts on the residents here in Methuen. As somebody was just talking about 
this wonderful building, we have a lot of great pieces of land. Unfortunately, it seems 
like being born and raised here, a lot of those pieces of land are being sold for 
development. It would be wonderful to be able to keep those lands and keep those 
environments for us, our families, and our and also the animals that we share the planet 
with. My hope is that you please take into consideration what he is asking but also look 
at the broader spectrum of what those impacts could potentially have on our residents. 
Lowell and some other places are having a very hard time with the impacts. As 
somebody who is a bit disabled myself, as I have tinnitus in both of my ears, I can't even 
imagine what it would be like to be near a Humming data center day in and day out. 
There are places that have been here before, a data center where potentially go up. A 
situation of price crossing is we have a condominium, but we have the airport, and the 
airport creates a lot of noise. What we were told was the airport preceded the 
condominium. What we have today before us is that we have neighborhoods that have 
preceded this potential data center that would or would not be going in. I would 
encourage you guys to please look at the impact on the life of people in their homes, and 
what it could do to them, and the landscape, and the beautiful environment that we have 
here, and not to let that be destroyed. So, I appreciate you all listening to me. Thank 
you.” 
• Jack Fleming, Albion Street, Methuen – “I'm Jack Fleming. I live on Albion Street, 
and I'm with her. Absolutely, data centers, no way. Lowell's having all sorts of problems 
with other parts of the country and having problems with them, just like these flock 
cameras that are all over the place. Twelve cities are taking them out now, but we have 
them. You know, if I had a chance to vote on the flock cameras, I would have been a no 
on that, too. That's all I've really got to say about it.” 
• Bob Leucano, New Hill Road, Methuen – “Yes, my name is Bob Leucano. I live on 
New Hill Road on the west side of Methuen. A couple things I'm curious about is we 
were talking about the data centers. Why was there no communication? Nobody knows 
about this, that this meeting was going to discuss the data centers. When they were 
talking about redoing Route 110, which goes by my house, they came around going 
house to house and gave a pamphlet so that we'd know there was a meeting at that time 
in Dracut to talk about the redoing of Route 110. This, absolutely nobody knew 
anything about this, all right? And second, the governor signed an executive order today 
to make it so that the town can refuse to have a data center. So, I don't even know why 
we're discussing this and why we're not just saying we don't want it. The amount of hell 
that's going on in Lowell right now, you see, watch the news. There's one guy that says 
he has to live next to this thing. He wished that the governor had signed this way before 
they built the thing. So, you can really stop it if you want to. I don't know what the 
advantages of it are, why we would want to do something that's going to tax our water, 
electricity, and everything else. I have no idea. I don't know what the advantage is to 
letting this thing come into Methuen. People don't want them. Maybe there should be 
some type of special election or something saying to the residents, you want to let this 
in? Because I think you'll find that if you do that, you're going to have people saying, no, 
we don't want it. And so, as the City Council, you should be listening to what the

today. You can stop it just by saying, no, we don't want it. Thank you.” 
  
5. Organizational Business - none

• Thursday, August 13, 2026 Special Meeting – Motion to accept by Clr. DiZoglio,

7. Proclamations/Correspondence: none 
 
8. Consideration of Appointments:     
• Matteo Zingales – Zoning Board of Appeals (currently serving as an alternate) - Motion 
to appoint by Clr. Pesce, seconded by Clr. Valley – Discussion – Chair Soto 
recognized Clr. DiZoglio, “Through you Madam Chair. So, I looked at Mr. I'm sorry if I 
pronounced his name wrong. I think he's well qualified for the position, but what I have 
an issue with is that he owns a business in Methuen where he's a realtor and if he was to 
approve zoning in Methuen, we can't say to him that you can't sell those properties. And 
to me, and I'm not saying he is that type of person, I just think also knowing people in 
the city of Methuen where they see that, they might say we're appointing people that 
might not be in the best interest of Methuen, especially development. That's why I'm not 
going to say I'm not going to vote yes on it but I'm not going to vote no on it. I'm just 
going to vote present on it.” Chair Soto recognized Clr. Pesce, “I'd just like to weigh in. I 
think potentially having a realtor on the Zoning Board of Appeals would offer a 
perspective that might be needed and I just want to remind Councilor DiZoglio that 
everybody who serves on a board has a duty and the solicitor I'm sure can back me up to 
recuse themselves if they have a conflict of interest. So, there should never be an instance 
where someone is benefiting from whatever decision they're making no matter what 
board they're on. That's a question of ethics not, you know, it's a rule.” Chair Soto 
recognized Clr. Marsan, “I just want to say that knowing that our chair of the Zoning 
Board just stepped down last week after his last meeting, I think it's imperative that we 
have more people, full-time guys, people on this board. I know Mr. Mateo and I believe 
Mr. Zingales and I feel very confident that he would step down if there was a conflict. A 
lot of the zoning issues are, you know, variances for setbacks and such things like that. 
So, it's not, it doesn't have to do with selling homes and, you know, that's the Planning 
Board where they, you know, subdivide land and do things like that. So, I just think this 
is a good fit for our board. Thank you.” Chair Soto recognized Clr. Valley, “Thank you, 
Madam Chair. Point of information, Councilor DiZoglio, I don't think Mr. Zingales is a 
licensed real estate agent or broker. He works for the company but he's not an agent. He 
oversees the operations of the company but he's not a salesperson. He's an architect.” 
Chair Soto recognized Clr. Drew, “Thank you, Madam Chair. Reading this, I think 
having an architect on the Zoning Board would be a great asset to the community. Just 
for full transparency, things not to make anything odd, you are listed as a point of

9. Presentations/Projects/Department Updates – Chair Soto said, “I want to let you guys 
know that the next meeting, we go back to a regular schedule of two meetings a month. 
Next Regular City Council meeting (on September 21st), we do have a GLTS workshop at 6 
p.m. and then we will have a presentation from the Searles Estate for 10 minutes at the next 
meeting. We circulated the Mayor's written Mayor’s Report. He had a conflict on today's

10.  Mayor’s Report – Mayor Beauregard submitted his Mayor’s Report in writing. 
11. CAFO Report – Chair Soto said, “If you feel that you need to move on something or table 
it until the Mayor's in front of you, please do so. And from that, from there, I'll go to the CAFO 
report. And then when we go to request of Councilors, what I'd like you guys to do, because the 
Mayor isn't here, unless we're going to have the Chief of Staff stand up and give you updates. I'd 
like you to elaborate if there's anything you want me to add to any of these or any changes or if 
you wanted to explain any reasoning.” Chair Soto recognized CAFO Maggie Duprey, “Thank 
you. So just quickly, the request for the Searles update on the expenses and revenues, there's 
really no change there, aside from minimal utility costs. Still there are no big changes there. As 
far as the back taxes question, I just have a follow-up question so that I can get the right thing to 
you. Are you looking specifically about tax title?” Clr. Drew said, “In, I believe it was January 
or February, we had what was brought to us, commercial properties that were in arrears along 
with residential homes. We had a third party going after all these different items. I'm just trying 
to see what's still pending, what have we been able to bring whole, and what's still out there? 
Have we made any sort of movement on any of these items? How much is still out there? 
Because last time I looked, it was significant. I believe it was like $7 million. Just want to know, 
have we brought in $10? Have we brought in $10 million? I just don't know where that stands, 
and I've just been following up over the last 10 there for six months. I figured this would be a 
good time to start looking at it.” CAFO Duprey said, “Yes, absolutely. I don't have anything for 
you tonight. I just wanted to make sure I understood. I believe last time I gave a detail of all of 
the properties. So I'll do the same thing this time so that you can kind of compare what that 
looks like, but I'll also do a little summary of what that looks like. It will include the actual tax

be in there. But I'll give you a similar report so that it's apples to apples. I'll send that to you, and

point in September. If we can maybe coordinate that and have that so we can digest it a little bit 
before the next meeting, I think that would be something so we can have some ideas of where 
we're heading in our financial outlook on the city.” CAFO Duprey said, “Yes, I'll have the 
report out to you this week, so that shouldn't be a problem.” Chair Soto said, “If I may, it may

be prudent to ask the Chair of the Finance Committee to maybe have the Tax Collector join you 
guys for that meeting and see. I mean, that's just a suggestion.” CAFO Duprey said, “I just 
wanted to give you two quick updates. One is we've talked here about increasing department 
fees. One of the Departments that we talked about specifically was Building. I talked to Caeli 
today and her department have been working very diligently on going through those and 
coming up with a proposal. So, they're looking at we're doing final reviews of that internally and 
hope to have it to Council for changes in the next couple of meetings. So just so that is an 
update. And the other thing I wanted to update you, I did provide an ARPA status report, and I 
did that because I really just wanted, you know, we're now in that approaching that last part of 
the year, and ARPA funds do need to be spent, completely spent, done by the end of this 
December. So, I know we've been talking about ARPA funds for literally four or five years at 
this point, and we're in that home stretch. So, I just thought it was important to provide you 
where we're at. We have spent 93% of our $46 million, which is fantastic. And we do have 
another 6.5% that's obligated and in the process of being spent. Right now, we only anticipate 
about half of 1% being returned to the state, which is a similar number to what we've been, you 
know, providing the Council already. And those are really driven by, we had the ARPA 
construction manager, that situation. And so, we had money left on the table there that, at that 
point, we couldn't reallocate. But minor changes, things not spent on some of these projects, but 
the majority, 99.5% of these funds are scheduled to be spent before the end of December. So, I'll 
keep you updated as we go. But I just wanted to kind of bring that back because that deadline is 
coming up.” Chair Soto recognized Clr. DiZoglio, “So yeah, I was just wondering to you, 
Madam Chair, to the CAFO, what is the update of the barrel fees that have we retained?” 
CAFO Duprey said, “I don't have an update on that.” Clr. DiZoglio said, “Well, through you, 
Madam Chair. So, we decided back in May, when we did this whole resolution, we sat here, we 
were promised reports every week regarding the tonnage and the barrel fees. Now it's been two 
meetings where we either get the same or we don't get any report. I don't understand where 
we're in the crisis that we're in, and you have admitted to this too as well, that where it comes to 
revenue, it seems like we're not trying to receive that. And just the other day, I received a call 
from a woman that was said to me, Mr. DiZoglio, I have not received my barrel fee. I knew I 
had to pay one and come to find out she was missing a letter in her email, which is funny 
because that email that she put in was an active email. So, someone from wherever it was 
getting an email saying they had to pay $100 barrel fee and she wasn't getting it. You guys have 
a list of barrels with a number, address, and an email. I don't understand with 1,336 people that 
have extra barrels, where a person can't sit down, do an email, and if not, no response, make 
cold calling. I don't understand why this is an issue. And I know everybody's looking at me and 
saying things like, Mr. DiZoglio, I don't understand why you're so bent out about this. Madam
